title: Pre-Purchase Ship Inspection Auckland | Wharves & Calliope Dock
description: Pre-purchase inspection in Auckland for ship buyers: car carriers and feeders at the wharves, trawlers in Calliope Dock, ferries and workboats on hardstands.
h1: Buying a Ship in Auckland: Pre-Purchase Inspection at the Wharves, in Calliope Dock or on the Hardstand
intro: Auckland is a long way from most buyers, and a ship sold there often faces a long delivery voyage, to the Pacific islands, back to Asia or round the New Zealand coast. Atlantis gives the buyer measured evidence before the deal closes: structure, coatings, spot thickness, crack checks and machinery readings on car carriers and feeders at the Waitematā wharves, on trawlers in the Calliope Dock at Devonport, and on ferries and workboats lifted out at the marine yards. The team travels from India to Auckland for each inspection, usually through an Asian or Australian hub, once the visa is granted.

highlights.p: A ship bought in Auckland may face weeks of open ocean before she reaches her new trade. The inspection looks hardest at what that passage will test: hull and deck integrity, hatch and door closures, steering gear and the machinery that has to keep running without a break.

When a seller docks a deep-water trawler in the Calliope Dock before handover, the buyer can have the bottom, sea chests and stern gauged from the dock floor, which says far more than an inspection afloat about a hull that works in heavy southern weather.

Older car carriers are often sold after years on the vehicle run from Asia. During discharge at a multi-cargo wharf, cleared decks, ramps and hoistable panels can be examined while vehicles still move on other levels, with the chief officer deciding where the team may go.

sections.h: Where can a buyer inspect a ship in Auckland?
p: Most buyers' inspections take place at the city wharves, because that is where the ships are when they are offered. A container feeder exchanging boxes at the Fergusson Container Terminal stays for about a day, so the visit covers the deck, coamings, whichever ballast tanks the ship can release and the engine room. Car carriers, cement ships and general cargo vessels discharge at the multi-cargo wharves, Bledisloe among them, and a car carrier's decks open up level by level as the vehicles leave.

For a dry hull, the Calliope Dock at Devonport is the only graving dock in the city. It sits inside the naval base, is leased to Babcock and takes commercial vessels such as trawlers and superyachts when naval work allows, so a seller who docks a vessel there before handover gives the buyer the bottom, sea chests and stern to examine from the dock floor. Visitors follow the dock operator's site access process. Ferries, fishing boats and workboats are lifted out onto the hardstands of the Wynyard Quarter yards and other harbour boatyards.

Ships waiting at anchor in the inner Hauraki Gulf can be reached by launch through the agent, but strong westerlies or north-easterlies can halt transfers, and a berth may come free sooner than expected. For a buyer with a fixed window under the sale terms, the anchorage is a fallback rather than the plan. Upgrades to the Bledisloe North and Fergusson North wharves will move some berths around in the coming years, which makes the agent's confirmation of where the ship will lie all the more important.
list: Fergusson Container Terminal: deck, coamings, releasable tanks and engine room on feeders and container ships
Multi-cargo wharves including Bledisloe: car carriers, cement ships and general cargo vessels during discharge
Calliope Dock, Devonport: bottom, sea chests and stern of trawlers, superyachts and similar vessels
Wynyard Quarter and other marine yards: ferries, fishing boats and workboats on the hardstand
Inner Hauraki Gulf anchorages: tanks and holds reached by launch, weather and agent permitting

sections.h: Which ships change hands in Auckland, and what should a buyer check on each?
p: Car carriers that have spent years on the run from Japan and other Asian factories are often sold on, for further trading or for recycling. The buyer's questions concern the parts of the ship that are seldom opened: double-bottom and side ballast tanks, deckheads under the upper car decks where condensation drips and corrodes, hoistable deck panels and their supports, and the hinges, locking gear and surrounding structure of the stern ramp and side doors.

Coastal general cargo and multipurpose ships are bought for the Pacific islands trade and for the New Zealand coast, frequently by operators who will run them far from any repair yard. Hatch covers, cranes and their pedestals, double-bottom tanks and the steering gear deserve close attention, because a defect found after delivery may have to be lived with for a long time. Deep-water trawlers bring their own issues: bow structure that takes heavy weather on the southern grounds, insulated fish holds and freezer spaces that hide the steel, and refrigeration plant whose condition shows in running readings.

Harbour ferries, launches and workboats, many of them with aluminium hulls, change hands between New Zealand operators, and superyachts that spend the summer in New Zealand waters are sometimes sold while refitting in Auckland. For a superyacht the inspection keeps to what it measures well, namely hull and tank readings, crack checks and machinery condition; it is not a valuation and does not judge interiors or finishes.

sections.h: Buying for New Zealand domestic service: surveys, MOSS and biosecurity
p: A vessel that will carry passengers or cargo commercially in New Zealand comes under the Maritime Operator Safety System. The operator needs a Maritime Transport Operator Certificate, and each vessel needs a current certificate of survey from a Recognised Surveyor, one of the surveyors Maritime New Zealand recognises for that work, with survey, certification and maintenance requirements set out in Maritime Rules Part 46. Our pre-purchase inspection answers a different question, the condition of hull and machinery before the buyer commits, and does not stand in for the Recognised Surveyor's work. With the buyer's agreement, the readings can be passed to that surveyor.

Biosecurity matters most when a buyer brings a vessel into New Zealand or keeps one there. Under the Ministry for Primary Industries' Craft Risk Management Standard for biofouling, a vessel staying less than 28 days and calling only at approved places of first arrival is treated as short-stay; a longer stay or other destinations put it in the long-stay category, which expects hull and niche areas to carry no fouling beyond a slime layer and goose barnacles, for example through inspection and cleaning within 30 days before arrival. When the inspection includes a docking, sea chests, gratings and other niche areas are photographed and recorded, giving the buyer a starting point; compliance itself rests with the owner and the cleaning provider.

sections.h: How is a pre-purchase inspection planned around an Auckland call or docking?
p: The journey shapes everything. The team flies from India to Auckland International Airport, usually changing in South-East Asia or Australia, and needs a New Zealand visa for short specialist work, supported by a letter from the buyer, the seller or the agent describing the job. Processing times vary, so the application goes in once the viewing is agreed, and the reference date is the berth or docking slot the seller's agent confirms.

At a wharf the stay is short, so spaces are ranked with the buyer's superintendent before arrival and entered in that order as the master releases them. On a car carrier, cleared decks come first and the ballast tanks follow once they have been ventilated and an entry permit issued. In the Calliope Dock the available time depends on the docking programme, so external readings and crack checks on the bottom and stern are done while the hull is dry and staged, and internal spaces follow. On a trawler, insulation and fish hold lining are opened only where the seller agrees, and the report states plainly which steel was not seen.

The season matters too. The summer cruise programme fills the city-centre berths, while winter brings fewer cruise calls and rougher weather in the outer Gulf, which makes launch boarding less dependable but frees quay space for ships lying idle while they are offered for sale. Whatever the setting, findings that could move the negotiation reach the buyer before the team leaves the ship.

sections.h: Worked scope: a multipurpose ship bought for the Pacific islands trade
p: The buyer will run the ship between small island ports with limited repair support, so the inspection concentrates on what would be hardest to put right later. Before arrival, the buyer's superintendent and our planner agree a ranked list: cargo holds once discharge at the multi-cargo wharf has finished, the double-bottom and wing ballast tanks the seller allows to be opened, hatch covers and their securing gear, crane pedestals and slewing ring foundations, and the steering gear flat.

On board, the holds are examined and gauged at frames, brackets and tank top as they become clear, crack checks are made at crane pedestal welds and hatch corners, and the cranes are run so their motors and gearboxes can be measured. In the engine room, generators and pumps are read under harbour load, the switchboard is thermally imaged and the main engine's records are gone through with the chief engineer. The buyer hears the day's decisive findings on board, and the report follows with readings located on the ship's drawings.

vessels: Coastal general cargo and multipurpose ships
Container feeders on coastal and Pacific islands loops
Bulk carriers in the cement trade
codes: Norwegian Saleform 2012 and SALEFORM 2025 – inspection by the buyers
IACS UR Z7 – hull classification surveys and coating condition terms
Maritime Rules Part 46 – surveys, certification and maintenance of New Zealand ships
Craft Risk Management Standard: Biofouling on Vessels Arriving to New Zealand
ASTM E797 – pulse-echo contact ultrasonic thickness measurement
deliverables: Before the team leaves: a summary of anything likely to alter the buyer's decision
Hold, tank, deck and closure condition, with spot readings marked on the drawings
Dock-floor readings of bottom, sea chests and stern when the vessel is docked
Crack-check results at crane pedestals, ramp hinges, engine bearers and other fatigue details
Machinery vibration and thermal readings, including cranes and refrigeration plant where they are run
List of covered, closed or loaded areas that could not be inspected, with the reason

faqs.q: Can a buyer inspect a trawler's fish hold in Auckland without removing the insulation?
faqs.a: Only in part. Insulation and lining hide most of the hold's steel, so without opening up the inspection relies on whatever panels are already off, on readings from adjacent tanks and, in dock, on shell readings taken from outside. Under the usual sale terms nothing is opened without the seller's consent, so the report lists the areas that stayed covered and says what the buyer could not learn about them.

faqs.q: Can the Calliope Dock be booked for a pre-purchase docking?
faqs.a: The seller or owner books the dock with its operator, and naval work has priority, so a docking for a sale has to fit around that programme. Trawlers, superyachts and other vessels that suit the dock use it; most merchant ships are too large and dock in Asia instead. When a seller does dock a vessel there, we plan the inspection to make full use of the hours while the hull is dry.

faqs.q: Does a pre-purchase inspection replace the Recognised Surveyor's survey for a New Zealand domestic vessel?
faqs.a: No. A vessel operating commercially within New Zealand needs a current certificate of survey from a Recognised Surveyor under the Maritime Operator Safety System, and that remains the surveyor's responsibility. Our inspection is the buyer's evidence of condition before the deal closes. Readings and photographs can be shared with the Recognised Surveyor if the buyer wants, but they do not replace the certification survey.

faqs.q: Can you inspect an aluminium ferry or workboat for a buyer in Auckland?
faqs.a: Yes, ideally while it sits on a hardstand at one of the harbour's marine yards. Out of the water, the hull plating can be gauged with the instrument calibrated for aluminium, and welds at engine bearers, jet or propeller mountings and the hull-to-deck joint can be checked with dye penetrant, since magnetic particle testing does not work on aluminium. Engines and gearboxes are measured running if the seller can arrange it.

faqs.q: Will the classification society credit thickness readings from an Auckland pre-purchase inspection?
faqs.a: No. Class will only count readings towards a survey when they come from a firm its own society has accepted under IACS UR Z17, and Atlantis's applications to DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for that approval are still in progress. A buyer's inspection does not need class credit: its readings support the decision and are set against the class records the seller authorises the society to release.

faqs.q: How do New Zealand biosecurity rules affect a ship bought in Auckland?
faqs.a: For a ship that keeps trading internationally and calls only briefly, little changes. The rules bite when the new owner plans a long stay, a refit or visits to places not approved for first arrival, because the vessel then has to meet the long-stay biofouling requirement. A docking inspection records the condition of the hull and niche areas, which helps the buyer plan cleaning, but compliance rests with the owner.
